A set of values that measure the rate of mortality or death is known as mortality indicators.

question: Which of the following is a mortality indicator?

correctAnswer: C. Number of days of restricted activity
explanationHtml:
Number of days of restricted activity is a disability indicator.

Morbidity is defined as public health outcomes focusing on diseases, traumas, or injury. Morbidity indicators can be used to measure the overall health and extent of healthcare utilisation in a given population.

Disability is defined as public health outcomes related to health conditions that include limitations in personal activities and societal participation. There are two types of disability indicators as follows:

  • Event type indicators-
    • Number of days of restricted activity
    • Bed disability days
    • Work loss days (or school loss days) within a specified period
  • Person type indicators-
    • Limitation of mobility: e.g confined to bed
    • Limitation of activity: e.g limitation to perform the basic activities of daily living such as eating and going to the toilet

options.text: Number of days of restricted activity

question: An epidemiologist is tasked with measuring the overall health status of a community using a morbidity indicator. Which of the following indicators will she not use?

explanationHtml:
HALE (Health Adjusted Life Expectancy) is an indicator that can be used to estimate the number of years a newborn is expected to live in full health based on the current rates of ill health and mortality.

HALE is calculated using the life expectancy at birth with an adjustment for time spent in poor health. It captures both fatal and non-fatal health outcomes of average levels of population health. It is also sensitive to changes over time or differences between countries in the distribution of health states.

Sullivan's index is also known as disability-free life expectancy (DFLE) or active life expectancy. It is the average number of years an individual is expected to live free of disability if the current patterns of mortality and disability continue to apply. It doesn’t take into account premature death. As HALE includes not just disability but the larger definition of poor health, it is a better option with respect to the question.
question: Which of the following indicators can be used to estimate the number of years a newborn would be expected to live in full health based on the current rates of ill health and mortality?

explanationHtml:
The proportional mortality rate is the simplest measure of estimating the burden of disease in the community. It signifies the proportion of all deaths that can be attributed to the disease.

It is calculated as follows:

Proportional mortality rate of a disease = (No. of deaths due to that disease in the year/ Total no. of deaths in the year) *100.

Option A: Case fatality rate measures the risk of persons dying from a certain disease within a given time period. It measures the killing power of a disease. It is used to link mortality to morbidity.

Option B: Incidence measures the rate at which new cases are occurring in a population. It is not influenced by the duration of the disease. The use of incidence is generally restricted to acute diseases.

Option C: Crude death rate is considered a fair indicator of the comparative health of the people. It is the rate of total deaths in a year compared to the mid-year population.
question: While assessing the health needs of a community, an epidemiologist is tasked with estimating the burden of cholera in the area. Which of the following is the simplest measure he can use?

explanationHtml:
Disability adjusted life years (DALY) is the best measure of the overall burden of a disease in a defined population. It is also the best measure of the effectiveness of interventions.

DALY is calculated as - Years of lost life prematurely (YLL) + Years lost to disability (YLD). It can measure both mortality and disability together.

As DALY is affected by premature loss of life, conditions that affect younger individuals like road traffic accidents have a high DALY. In comparison to this, Alzheimer's disease has a lower DALY as it is a disease that mostly develops during old age and so has a lower YLL.

Health utilisation rates include:

Lifestyle is a behavioural and socio-cultural determinant of health. It is not a socio-economic determinant.

Socio-economic determinants of health are the following:

  • Economic status (per capita GNP)
  • Education
  • Occupation
  • Political system

Lifestyle is simply the way people live. It reflects our social values, attitudes, and activities. It is composed of:

  • Cultural patterns (daily nutrition, superstitions)
  • Behavioral patterns (personal hygiene, sedentary life)
  • Lifelong personal habits (e.g. smoking, alcoholism)

Lifestyle is learned by social interaction with parents, siblings, friends, school, and mass media.

Our political system determines our health. It can help shape community health services with regards to resource allocation, manpower policy, choice of technology, and the degree to which these services are made available & accessible to all segments of the society.

The percentage of GDP spent on health is an indicator of political commitment. WHO recommends at least 5% of GDP to be spent on health care. India spends about 2.1 % of its GDP on health(budget 2022-23).

correctAnswer: D. It includes provision of free health camps by the government
explanationHtml:
The provision of free health camps by the government is a concept of state medicine.

Health does not merely mean the absence of disease or provision of diagnostic, curative, and preventive services. It is a state of physical, mental, and social well-being.

The state of positive health is based on the idea of perfect functioning of the body and mind. According to this concept, health is:

  • Biologically a state in which every cell and organ in the body is functioning at optimum capacity
  • Psychologically a state in which the individual feels a sense of perfect well-being and mastery over his environment
  • Socially a state in which the individual's capacities for participation in the social system are optimal

This concept is too idealistic and can never become a reality. Humans can never be so perfectly adapted to the environment because everything in our life is subject to change.

As the goal of positive health is unattainable, a broader concept of improving the quality of life has emerged. This highlights that positive health depends on medical action and also on economic, cultural, and social factors in the community.

Non-infectious conditions can also show cyclical trends.

Random error arises when a value of the sample measurement diverges, due to chance alone, from that of the true population value. They can never be completely eliminated.

Placebo 1804 (c) 13421 (d) 15225 (c+d)

question: Which among the following is the weakest study design to prove causation?

Case-control and cohort studies have a moderate ability to provide evidence for causality. Ecological studies or correlational studies are considered as the weakest study design in this aspect.

question: Which of the following study designs is the best to prove causation?

explanationHtml:
In a randomized controlled trial (RCT), the clinician has no control over the allocation of participants in each group. The main purpose behind randomisation is to eliminate selection bias.

This allows comparability between the study and the control population. The process of randomisation is done after the selection of study subjects. As a result, the sample may not be referenced to all broader population groups. The clinician cannot predict which treatment each subject will receive.

question: In a clinical trial to evaluate a drug, randomisation was done before starting the trial. Which of the following is true?

Note: Per-protocol analysis is a comparison of treatment groups that include only those patients who completed the treatment originally allocated to them. Hence, comparability between the study and control group is limited and randomisation is lost.

question: A researcher decided to use double-blinding in his trial evaluating two new therapies for cystic fibrosis. What is the characteristic feature of this concept?

explanationHtml:
A cross-over study would be the best method to ensure comparability between the experimental and control group while eliminating ethical concerns.

In a cross over study design, patients are randomly assigned to the study and control group, and then after a period of time, their groups are switched. Here, each patient serves as his/her own control which allows for maximum comparability. A cross over study design is ethically superior to a concurrent parallel study since each patient receives both the placebo and the treatment benefits.

In a concurrent parallel study design, comparisons are made between two randomly assigned groups and there is no switching of groups.

Quasi-experiments are studies that aim to evaluate interventions but that do not use randomization. The lack of randomisation is the major weakness of quasi trials. The comparability in a quasi trial is limited.

A per-protocol analysis is a comparison of treatment groups that include only those patients who completed the treatment originally allocated. Hence, comparability is limited.
question: In a clinical trial, what would be the best study design that ensures comparability between experimental and control groups while eliminating ethical concerns?

  • Monitoring of adverse reactions

Phase II involves therapeutic exploration which is the evaluation of the efficacy of the drug and dose-ranging (determination of the optimum tolerated dose).
question: A new drug for multiple sclerosis is undergoing clinical trials where its therapeutic efficacy is being confirmed and adverse reactions are being monitored. Which of the following phases is the drug most likely in?

question: In which of the following phases is the maximum drug failure rate seen?

Phase I trials are usually performed on healthy volunteers to check the safety and pharmacokinetic properties of a drug. The participants in this phase do not gain any direct health benefits from taking part. It is a type of RCT and preventive trial. If the outcome is a significant reduction in disease then the association of that habit or agent to the disease is strengthened.

A trial of aetiological agents is an experimental epidemiological study to confirm or refute an aetiological hypothesis.

Clinical trials, for the most part, have been concerned with evaluating therapeutic agents, mainly drugs.

An uncontrolled trial is an example of a non-randomised trial where there is no control group for comparison.

Researchers find situations where two groups have been naturally created (eg.,smokers and non-smokers). Then, they test their hypotheses on these groups in the form of a natural experiment.

Non-randomized trials include:

  • Natural experiments
  • Before and after comparison studies

It is a type of zoonoses. Zoonoses are diseases that are transmitted between vertebrate animals and humans.

Other types of zoonoses include:

  • Anthropozoonoses - infections that are transmitted to man from vertebrates. E.g., Rabies, plague etc.
  • Zooanthroponoses - infections that are transmitted to vertebrates from humans. E.g., Human tuberculosis in cattle.

Epizootic disease refers to an outbreak or epidemic of a disease in an animal population, often with the implication that it may also affect human populations. Enzootic disease is an endemic occurring in animals.

Enzootic diseases are those which are endemic in animals. E.g, anthrax, brucellosis.

Epidemic refers to an increase, often sudden, in the number of cases of a disease above what is normally expected in that population in that area.

Pandemic is an epidemic occurring over a wide area, crossing international boundaries, and usually affecting a large number of people.

An endemic disease is a disease that is present constantly in a population or in a given area without importation from outside. E.g, kala-azar in Bihar.

A hyperendemic disease is a disease that is constantly present at high incidence and prevalence among all groups in a population. E.g, dengue in India.

A syndemic is the aggregation of two or more concurrent or sequential epidemics or disease clusters in a population with biological interactions, which exacerbate the prognosis and burden of disease. It is also known as a synergistic epidemic.

Note: Quasiendemic is not a term used in infectious disease epidemiology.

explanationHtml:
Subclinical infection is not seen in measles. It always causes the development of overt signs and symptoms.

Subclinical infection refers to an inapparent, covert, missed or abortive case. The host harbours and sheds the infectious agent but does not develop signs and symptoms of the disease.

Subclinical infections are seen in diseases like:

  • Hepatitis A
  • Diphtheria
  • Japanese encephalitis
  • Rubella

Subclinical infections can only be detected by laboratory tests. They frequently occur during a person’s lifetime and are responsible for the immunity shown by humans to a variety of disease-producing microbes.

Note: Subclinical cases should be differentiated from latent infections. In a latent infection, the host does not shed the organism but it lies dormant without signs and symptoms.

question: In which of the following diseases is subclinical infection not seen?

explanationHtml:
The host does not shed the infectious organism in case of a latent infection. This is defined as a state in which the host does not show signs and symptoms of the disease and does not shed the organism.

It can be seen in conditions like herpes simplex, ancylostomiasis, infections due to slow viruses, Brill-Zinsser disease, etc.

Subclinical infection is a state where the host harbours the infectious agent without developing signs and symptoms but sheds the infectious agent. This state is seen in conditions like hepatitis A, rubella, mumps, etc.

Healthy carriers are those who had subclinical infections and later developed a carrier state without suffering from the overt disease. This state is seen in: (mnemonic: CM - DPT)

  • Cholera
  • Meningitis
  • Diphtheria
  • Polio
  • Typhoid

Convalescent carriers are those which shed the infectious agent during the convalescent phase/recovery phase. Such carriers are seen in diphtheria, typhoid, cholera, pertussis, etc.

A suspect case refers to a patient who has all the features of the disease but has not been diagnosed with it yet.

explanationHtml:
The median incubation period is the time required for 50% of the cases to occur following exposure. The median incubation period of COVID-19 of approximately 5 days.

Incubation period is the time interval between invasion of the infectious agent and the appearance of the first symptom or sign in the body. It is termed as the latent period in non-infectious diseases.

Incubation period depends upon:

  • Generation time of pathogen
  • Portal of entry
  • Infective dose
  • Individual susceptibility

Incubation period is useful for :

  • Tracing the source of infection and contacts.
  • Determining the period of surveillance or quarantine.
  • Planning immunization.
  • Identification of point source or propagated epidemics.
  • Determining the prognosis.

The time interval between the onset of the primary case and the secondary case is called serial interval.

By collecting information about a whole series of such disease onsets, the distribution of the secondary cases can be made. From this information, an approximation of the incubation period can be done.

Lead time/lead interval refers to the period between the first possible time of detection and the usual time of diagnosis.

Incubatory interval/ incubation period refers to the time period between invasion of a pathogen to appearance of the first sign or symptom.

Latent interval/ latent period refers to the period between disease initiation to detection of the disease. It is usually used for non-infectious diseases and is equivalent to the incubation period.

A reservoir is the environment (e.g. soil, humans, animals, water, etc.) where the infectious agent grows and multiplies (natural habitat) and from where it can be transmitted to a susceptible host.

A source is an animal, object, human or substance which acts as an immediate mode of transmission and may or may not be a part of the reservoir.

Chronic carriers are those who shed or excrete the organism for indefinite periods.

Carriers are classified into chronic carriers and temporary carriers based on the duration.

Organisms may be shed continuously or intermittently in chronic carriers. The duration of the carrier state also depends on the disease. Chronic carrier state is seen in typhoid, hepatitis B, gonorrhea, malaria, etc.

Temporary carriers are classified into:

  • Incubatory carriers - Those that shed the organism during the incubation period of the disease, especially during the later parts of it. It is seen in measles, mumps, polio, etc.
  • Healthy carriers - Those who suffer from subclinical infections and develop a carrier state without developing the overt disease. It is seen in polio, meningococcal meningitis, cholera, diphtheria, etc.
  • Convalescent carriers - Those that shed the organism during recovery or convalescence. It is seen in typhoid.

Paradoxical carrier refers to a carrier who acquires the pathogen from another carrier.

explanationHtml:
Droplet nuclei can travel as far as 6 feet, whereas a droplet (particle > 5μm) travels <30-60cm, as recent studies have shown.

Droplets are a mode of direct transmission of infectious agents. They are formed from saliva and nasopharyngeal secretions released during coughing, sneezing, or speaking into the surrounding atmosphere. The expelled droplets may impinge directly upon the conjunctiva, oro-respiratory mucosa or skin of close contact. This mode of transmission is seen in common cold, diphtheria, etc.

Proper basic ventilation and prevention of overcrowding reduce the potential for this type of transmission.

question: Which among the following is false about droplet transmission?

explanationHtml:
Droplet nuclei are sized less than or equal to 5 microns.

They may be formed by evaporation of droplets coughed or sneezed into the air or be generated purposefully by a variety of atomizing devices (aerosols). They are capable of indirect airborne transmission of diseases like tuberculosis, influenza, chickenpox, measles, etc.

The droplet nuclei may remain airborne for long periods of time, some retaining and others losing infectivity or virulence. These small particles when inhaled are capable of reaching the alveoli and getting retained there.
question: What is the maximum size of airborne droplet nuclei?

explanationHtml:
Airborne transmission by droplet nuclei is not a method of direct transmission of diseases.

It is a method of indirect transmission of diseases.

Droplet nuclei are tiny particles of size 1-5 microns range that may be formed by either due to evaporation of droplets coughed or sneezed into the air or are formed from aerosols.

These droplet nuclei remain airborne for long periods of time and can transmit diseases like tuberculosis, influenza, chickenpox, measles, Q fever and other respiratory infections.

Droplet transmission, vertical transmission, and contact with soil are methods of direct transmission of diseases.

Differences between droplet and droplet nuclei are summarised below:

DROPLET NUCLEI DROPLET
Indirect transmission Direct transmission
It is the residue from evaporated droplets It is produced while coughing, sneezing, talking
<5microns in diameter ≥5 microns in diameter
No need for close contact for transmission Requires closeness and direct contact for transmission

question: Which of the following is not a method of direct transmission of communicable diseases?

explanationHtml:

Vehicle-borne transmission is the transmission of infectious agents through food, water and biological products (blood, plasma etc.). Of these, food and water are more frequent vehicles of transmission because they are used by everyone.

Secondary attack rate measures the communicability of the disease.

question: Which of the following is false about specific human immunoglobulins?

correctAnswer: D. Production of antibody is slower
explanationHtml:
Production of antibodies is faster in secondary booster response.

Primary response is the immune response developed when an antigen is administered for the first time to a person who has never been exposed to it. There is a latent period of 3-10 days before antibodies appear in the blood.

Secondary booster response is the immune response elicited by a booster dose. In comparison to a primary immune response, it has a shorter latent period, faster production of antibodies, and an abundance of antibodies. The antibody response is maintained at higher levels for a longer period of time, and the antibody elicited tends to have a greater avidity or capacity to bind to the antigen.

question: Which of the following is not true about secondary booster immune response in comparison with primary response?

correctAnswer: A. Simultaneous administration of two live vaccines should be done in the same syringe
explanationHtml:
Simultaneous administration of vaccines is defined as administering more than one vaccine on the same clinic day, at different anatomic sites. They are not combined in the same syringe.

Simultaneous administration of the most widely used live and inactivated vaccines does not result in decreased antibody responses or increased rates of adverse reaction. However, in children with functional or anatomic asplenia pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) and Menactra brand meningococcal conjugate vaccines should not be administered at the same visit; separate these vaccines by at least 4 weeks.

Advantages of simultaneous administration of vaccines:

  • The organisms multiply in the host and thus, the antigenic dose is larger than what is injected.
  • They have all the major and minor antigenic components.

Live vaccines should not be administered to those with an immunocompromised state, since they may cause severe systemic disease by way of viremia/bacteriemia.

Note: If live vaccines are not given simultaneously, they must be spaced as follows-

  • The administration of two live parenteral vaccines or live intranasal influenza vaccines must be separated by at least 4 weeks (28 days).
  • If two live vaccines are given less than 4 weeks apart, the second vaccine should be repeated in four weeks. This is because the live vaccine given first can interfere with the second vaccine, and the person may not develop active immunity to the second vaccine.

Inactivated or killed vaccines are made from growing cultures of the organism and then inactivating them with heat or chemicals.They activate the channels of active immunity after injection and are less efficacious than live vaccines. Multiple doses or booster doses are usually required to produce an adequate antibody response.

Killed vaccines can be given to immune-compromised individuals and in pregnancy as the infective agent is inactivated and cannot grow.

Egg allergy is not an absolute contraindication to the administration of an inactivated or killed vaccine.

explanationHtml:

Thus, a limitation of these vaccines is that the immune responses are serotype-specific.

If these vaccines are conjugated with proteins, they are given the capability of eliciting a stronger immune response. Multivalent formulations of both polysaccharide-based vaccines and conjugated vaccines are required to achieve protection against multiple serotypes.

Concurrent disinfection is the application of disinfection methods after discharge of infectious material from a person or soiling. This includes disinfection of urine, faeces, vomit, contaminated linen, clothes, hands.

Terminal disinfection is done after the death of a patient or transfer or after cessation of isolation.

The Rideal-Walker coefficient helps in assessing the power of a disinfectant relative to phenol.

  • In-use test - determines whether the chosen disinfectant is effective in actual hospital use

Both sensitivity and specificity are higher in the test represented in pink (Test B) compared to the test represented in green (Test A).

Sensitivity is the proportion of all people with the disease who test positive. It is the probability of the test being positive when the disease is present.

Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN) or Sensitivity = 1 – false-negative rate.

Specificity is the proportion of all people without the disease who test negative. It is the probability of the test being negative when the disease is absent.

The simultaneous administration of hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) and hepatitis B vaccine is more efficacious than HBIG alone for the prevention of the carrier state in newborn babies of HBV-positive mothers.

HBIG does not interfere with the antibody response to the hepatitis B vaccine. This combined procedure is ideal both for postexposure prophylaxis of persons accidentally exposed to blood known to contain hepatitis B virus and for the prevention of the carrier state in the newborn babies of carrier mothers.

correctAnswer: A. Severe rotavirus infections are limited to children aged 5-7 years.
explanationHtml:
Severe rotavirus gastroenteritis is largely limited to children aged 6-24 months, not 5-7 years.

Rotavirus is the leading cause of severe, dehydrating diarrhea in children aged <5 years globally. In developing countries, 75% of the children acquire their first rotavirus infection in the first 12 months.

The universal occurrence of rotavirus infections shows that clean water supply and good hygiene are unlikely to have a substantial effect on virus transmission. In tropical areas, rotavirus diarrhea occurs throughout the year, increasing in frequency in drier, cooler climates.

Transmission is through the feco-oral route, person-to-person contact, or indirectly through fomites. Infected individuals shed very high concentrations of the virus for many days in their stool and vomit.

The antibody titers of all carriers are risen and positive till the person harbors the organism.

A cholera carrier is defined as an apparently healthy person excreting V.cholerae O1 in stools. Selective media and enrichment is needed for their diagnosis. In cholera, 4 types of carriers are described.

  1. Incubatory/Pre-Clinical carriers: The duration of carrier state is 1-5 days (incubation period). They present with symptoms later.
  2. Convalescent carriers: Recovered from an attack of cholera, continues to excrete vibrios for 2-3 weeks, due to ineffective antibiotic treatment.
  3. Contact/Health carrier: Due to subclinical infection contracted through a case or an infected environment, may excrete for 10 days.
  4. Chronic carriers: Gallbladder is infected, duration may be as long as 10 years.

explanationHtml:
In patients with cholera, if diarrhea persists after 48 hours of antibiotic therapy, resistance to the antibiotic should be suspected.

Treatment for cholera:

  • Rehydration therapy - is started immediately, either oral or intravenous.
  • Antibiotic therapy - As soon as vomiting has stopped (usually after 3-4 hours of rehydration). Fluoroquinolones, tetracycline, azithromycin, ampicillin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are commonly used.
  • Shock in diarrhea must be corrected by intravenous fluids only.

Antidiarrhoeals, cardiotonics, antiemetics, antispasmodics, and corticosteroids are not used.

question: Which of the following guidelines will you follow to treat a child diagnosed with cholera?

explanationHtml:
Tetracycline is the drug of choice for chemoprophylaxis of cholera.

It should be given for:

  • Adults - a 3-day period in a twice-daily dose of 500mg
  • Children (4-13 years) - 125mg
  • Children (0-3 years) - 50mg

Alternatively, the long-acting tetracycline (doxycycline) may be used for chemoprophylaxis, if the prevailing strains are not resistant. A single oral dose of doxycycline (300 mg for adults and 6 mg/kg for children under 15 years) has proved to be effective.

Chemoprophylaxis is advised only for household contacts or a closed community in which cholera has occurred.

question: Which of the following is the most effective prophylactic measure against cholera?

correctAnswer: A. Safe water supply and sanitation
explanationHtml:
Safe water supply and sanitation is the first step to be taken to decrease the incidence of cholera.

Steps taken to decrease the incidence of cholera include:

  • Safe water supply
  • Excreta disposal
  • Food sanitation
  • Disinfection
  • Early case detection

Cholera Vaccines: available in oral forms

  • Dukoral
  • Sanchol and mORCVAX
  • Euvichol
  • Vaxchora
  • CVD103-HgR - no longer produced

Sanchol and Euvichol are available for mass vaccination campaigns. The campaigns have been implemented in areas experiencing an outbreak, in areas at heightened vulnerability during humanitarian crises, and among populations living in highly endemic areas, known as hotspots.

Vaxchora is given for adults (18 – 64 years) who are traveling to an area of active cholera transmission, at least 10 days before the trip.

Mass chemoprophylaxis is not recommended for the control of cholera. This is because the drug's effect is only short-lived (a few days). Moreover, for preventing 1 case of cholera, around 10,000 individuals must be given the drug. Chemoprophylaxis is recommended for only household contacts of confirmed cases with tetracycline.

For disinfection, attention should be paid to the following: patient's stools and vomit; clothes and other contaminated personal items; the latrine, the patient's house, and neighborhood.

explanationHtml:
The number of cases and deaths due to cholera are to be reported daily and weekly till the area is declared free of cholera.

International health regulations for the notification of Cholera:

  • Cholera is notifiable to the WHO by the National Government within 24 hours of its occurrence.
  • The number of cases and deaths due to cholera are to be reported daily and weekly till the area is declared free of cholera.
  • When twice the incubation period (5 days) i.e. 10 days has elapsed since the death, recovery, or isolation of the last case, an area is declared free of cholera.
  • Mass prophylaxis is not advised in cholera, as it fails to stop the spread of the disease. Chemoprophylaxis is only advised for household contacts or a closed community.

question: A 5-year-old boy has had 15 episodes of loose stools in the last 24 hours and vomited twice in the last 4 hours. The child is restless and has sunken eyes. On examination, he is irritable but is drinking fluids. What is the optimal therapy for the child?

explanationHtml:
The freshly prepared ORS should not be used after 24 hours.

Guidelines for administering ORS:

After each loose stool, give:

Children <2 years of age 50-100 ml (1/4 to 1/2 large cup) of fluid
Children 2 - 10 years 100-200 ml (1/2 to one large cup)
Older children and adults As much fluid as they want
  • In every 1 to 2 minutes, 1 teaspoon should be administered to children younger than 2 years and frequent sips should be offered out of a cup for older children. Try to give the estimated required amount within a 4-hour period.
  • If the child vomits, wait for 10 minutes, then give a spoonful every 2 to 3 minutes.
  • If the child wants to drink more ORS solution than the estimated amount and does not vomit, there is no harm in feeding him/her more.
  • Continuation of breastfeeding should be done along with ORS solution administration in breast-fed children.

question: A 9-month-old baby with diarrhea is feeding well and is thirsty. Skin pinch when done returns in 2 seconds. What is the treatment?

correctAnswer: B. Unsalted water in which a cereal has been cooked
explanationHtml:
Unsalted water in which cereal has been cooked is not advisable for a child with diarrhoea.

If the WHO ORS mixture is not available, a simple mixture of 1 teaspoon of salt and 6 teaspoons of sugar must be dissolved in 1 L of drinking water and given to the child.

Fluids that do not contain salt in water, for eg: rice water, unsalted soup, yoghurt drinks, green coconut water, etc, are not preferred, although they may be used in cases where fluids which contain salt are unavailable. 3g/litre of salt must be added to such drinks before giving it to the child with diarrhoea.

The infant's usual diet of cereals, vegetables and other foods should be continued and never be diluted. The child should be given as much nutrient-rich food as acceptable.

Avoid the following:

  • Sweetened drinks with sugar, like commercial fruit juices and sweetened tea, as they lead to osmotic diarrhoea and hypernatremia.
  • Fluids with a stimulant and purgative effect like coffee and medicinal tea infusions.

Skin elasticity and pulse strength are the most helpful indicators for adequate intravenous rehydration.

The urine output may be unchanged even after 3-4 hours of adequate rehydration. Hence, it cannot be a criterion for continuous examination.

The initial rehydration must be fast until an easily palpable pulse is present. Reassess the patient every 1-2 hours.

After 1-2 liters of fluid have been infused, the drip should be slowed down till the blood pressure and pulse return to normal. Rehydration must be continued otherwise till all signs of dehydration have disappeared. ORS should be given when the patient can drink oral fluids.

Puffy eyelids are a sign of excess rehydration and intravenous fluids must be stopped when it occurs.

The bacteriological index (BI) of the given samples is 3.5

According to Ridley’s logarithmic scale,

  • 10 bacilli out of 100 oil immersion fields indicate an index of 1+
  • > 1000 bacilli out of average fields imply an index of 6+

The bacteriological index is calculated by adding the index from each site examined and dividing the total by the number of sites examined.

Hence, BI = (1+1+6+6) / 4

BI = 14/4

correctAnswer: B. Filters in cigarettes are protective against the development of CHD.
explanationHtml:
Filters are probably not protective against the development of coronary heart disease in smokers.

Smoking is a modifiable risk factor for coronary heart disease (CHD). The degree of risk is directly related to the number of cigarettes smoked per day. Several mechanisms have been suggested for this:

  • Carbon monoxide induced atherogenesis
  • Nicotine stimulation of adrenergic drive
  • Lipid metabolism with fall in levels of HDL

Cigarettes also increase the risk of sudden death in patients with CHD who are below 50 years of age. The risk of death from CHD decreases with the cessation of smoking. The risk declines quite substantially within one year of stopping smoking and more gradually thereafter until, after 10- 20 years, it is the same as that of non-smokers.

Risk factors for coronary heart disease are:

  • Modifiable:
    • Cigarette smoking
    • High blood pressure
    • Elevated serum cholesterol
    • Diabetes
    • Obesity
    • Sedentary habits
    • Stress
  • Non-modifiable:
    • Age
    • Sex
    • Family history
    • Genetic factors
    • Personality

Community level

correctAnswer: A. Slide (A) is more useful for estimating the parasite concentration
explanationHtml:
Slide (A) is a thin blood smear and slide (B) is a thick blood smear. Thin blood smears (slide A) are not more useful for estimating parasite concentration than thick smears. They are mainly used to detect the species of parasite.

Microscopy is the best method for the diagnosis of malaria due to its high sensitivity and specificity. Jaswant Singh Battacharya (JSB) stain is used for staining both thick and thin smears.

Thick smear is used to detect infection and estimate parasite concentration. The correct thickness is the thickness through which a newsprint is barely visible. It is prepared by slow-drying for 30 minutes, which leads to hemolysis and distortion of the plasmodia morphology. Hence, species cannot be detected.

Thin smear is used to identify the particular infecting species of Plasmodium. It is prepared by air drying for 10 minutes and fixed in methanol. Thus, the plasmodia morphology is not distorted.

explanationHtml:
Lymphatic filariasis will be considered eliminated when the children born after the initiation of the programme are free from antigenemia. Antigenemia refers to the presence of adult filaria worms in the human body.

According to the Elimination of Lymphatic Filariasis (ELF) Programme, there are two criteria to consider elimination of lymphatic filariasis:

  • Children born after the initiation of the elimination programme are free from circulating antigenemia.
  • The number of microfilaria carriers is <1%.

Following the failure to achieve ELF by 2015, the target set to eliminate lymphatic filariasis by WHO was 2020. To achieve the same WHO recommended the use of triple therapy for lymphatic filariasis. It incorporated ivermectin along with diethylcarbamazine (DEC) and albendazole instead of the traditional DEC and albendazole therapy, for the elimination of transmission of lymphatic filariasis.

In 2021, WHO released the 'Road Map for Neglected Tropical Diseases (2021–2030)'. Under this, lymphatic filariasis is targeted for elimination as a public health problem by 2030.

In February 2023, the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare in India launched a nationwide Sarva Dawa Sevan or Mass Drug Administration (MDA) campaign to eliminate LF by 2027, aiming to achieve this goal three years ahead of the global target.

The presence of new erythematous and tender subcutaneous nodules in a patient with leprosy indicates that he has developed type II lepra reaction. It is also known as Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL) and the first line of treatment is prednisolone.

Multi-drug therapy (MDT) should not be restarted in patients who develop lepra reactions after the completion of treatment.

Prednisolone is started at a dose of 40 mg per day and gradually tapered by 5 mg every 2 weeks. 'Prednisolone card' is given when treatment is started. If the patient becomes steroid-dependent, then clofazimine is added.

The key targets of the Global Leprosy Strategy 2021-2023 announced by WHO (Accelerating towards a leprosy-free world) are:

  • 120 countries reporting zero new autochthonous cases.
  • 70% reduction in the annual number of new cases detected.
  • 90% reduction in rate per million population of new cases with Grade 2 disability.
  • 90% reduction in rate per million children of new child cases with leprosy.

The current goal is the elimination of leprosy.

explanationHtml:
The two test protocol for the diagnosis of HIV consists of ELISA as the second test. If the initial ELISA is positive, a second ELISA is carried out. If the second ELISA is also positive, only then the case is reported to be positive.

Investigations involved in HIV testing strategies:

  1. ELISA/ rapid tests.
  2. Confirmatory tests with high specificity like western blot and line immunoassays are used in problem cases eg: indeterminate/ discordant cases of rapid tests.

In India, NACO provides western blot (WB) confirmatory testing only to resolve indeterminate results on previous serological testing. It is not used for routine confirmation after a positive result on screening tests. Drawbacks of WB include low rates of detection during acute HIV infection and misclassification of HIV-2 infection.

Note: The western blot is used as a confirmatory test after 2 indeterminate primary tests (ELISA). It is essentially the third test used and does not fit into the two test protocol.

The false statement about the Indian Hypertension Control Initiative is a 90% reduction in the prevalence of hypertension by the year 2025.

The IHCI is an initiative by the MoHFW, WHO, ICMR, and state governments to control hypertension in India. It has adopted the goal of “25 by 25” to reduce the prevalence of hypertension in India by 25% by 2025. The activities of IHCI are monitored by the cardiovascular health officers (CVHO's) at the state and district level and by the senior treatment supervisors (STS's) at the sub-district level. The IHCI has strengthened the prevention of hypertension by ensuring the provision of antihypertensive medications for 30 days to all patients registered under the IHCI.

The 5 components of IHCI are:

  1. Use of standardized hypertension treatment protocols approved by national and global policies.
  2. Availability of recommended protocol drugs to provide a regular and uninterrupted supply of medications.
  3. Task-sharing and team-based care involving nurses, health workers, and ASHAs to improve treatment compliance.
  4. Patient-centered services provide easy access to BP monitoring at Health & wellness centers and PHCs.
  5. Information systems that provide real-time BP monitoring to improve patient follow-ups: Use of the “Simple App” in all IHCI states.

*Note: Amlodipine, telmisartan, and chlorthalidone are the drugs of choice in the standardized treatment protocols of the IHCI.

POCSO Act defines a child as any person below eighteen years of age. It defines different forms of sexual abuse, including penetrative and non-penetrative assault, as well as sexual harassment and pornography.

The Act deems a sexual assault to be "aggravated" under certain circumstances, such as when the abused child is mentally ill or when the abuse is committed by a person in a position of trust or authority vis-à-vis the child, like a family member, police officer, teacher, or doctor.

Mass Drug Administration (MDA) is the administration of a drug to an entire concerned population irrespective of age and gender. Vitamin A prophylaxis is given under National Immunization Schedule (NIS) only to children up to 5 years. It is given as mass prophylaxis and not as a drug for treatment. Vitamin A as a treatment is given only to a child with features of vitamin A deficiency and such doses are not instituted to everyone in the community. Therefore, it is not considered under MDA.

The monetary benefit is measured in a cost-benefit analysis.

In cost-benefit analysis, the economic benefits of any program are compared with the cost of the program. The benefits are expressed in monetary terms to determine whether a given programme is economically sound and to select the best out of several alternate programmes.

The main drawback with this technique is that the benefits in the health field, as a result of a particular programme, cannot always be expressed in monetary terms. We generally express the benefit in terms of births or deaths prevented, or illness avoided or overcome.

In cost-effective analysis, the benefit is expressed in terms of results achieved. (Eg: number of lives saved or number of days free from disease).

Input-output analysis: how much input is needed to produce a unit amount of output. In the health field, input refers to all health service activities which consume resources (manpower, money, materials, and time); and output refers to useful outcomes such as cases treated, lives saved, or inoculations performed.

Network analysis: a network is a graphic plan of all events and activities to be completed in order to reach an end objective.

National Policy for Rare Diseases is a comprehensive policy for the prevention and management of rare diseases. The policy lists rare diseases under 3 groups:

  • Group 1: Disorders amenable to one-time curative treatment:
    • Disorders amenable to hematopoietic stem cell transplantation eg: lysosomal storage disorders
    • Disorders amenable to organ transplantation eg: glycogen storage disorders, urea cycle disorders, ADPKD, etc.
  • Group 2: Diseases requiring long term/ lifelong treatment having a relatively lower cost of treatment:
    • This group includes disorders managed with special dietary formulae/ hormone/ specific drugs. eg: phenylketonuria, osteogenesis imperfecta, etc.
  • Group 3: Diseases for which definitive treatment is available but treatment is lifelong or expensive:
    • This group includes diseases such as Pompe disease, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, etc.

The objectives of the policy are:

  • Lowering the high cost of treatment for rare diseases with an increased focus on indigenous research.
  • Creating a national hospital-based registry of rare diseases.
  • Early screening and prevention through primary and secondary health care infrastructure, and through counselling for the high-risk parents.

Subclinical folate deficiency is seen in up to 30% of North Indian pregnant women. Moreover, it may be masked by widespread iron deficiency. It is, for this reason, iron and folate supplementation is carried out in national programmes.

Clinical vitamin B12 deficiency is not commonly encountered, but subclinical cases might be seen in up to 30% of adults and children due to widespread restriction to consumption of vegetarian products only. Hence supplementing vitamin B12 is a good idea provided the cost factor is not an issue.

explanationHtml:
According to the Indian Academy of Paediatrics, catch-up vaccination of BCG is allowed up to 5 years of age. So, this patient should be administered the BCG vaccine straightaway.

The BCG vaccine is given intradermally at a dose of 0.1 ml in the left upper arm at the deltoid insertion site as soon as possible after birth. This vaccine is contraindicated in children with immunodeficiency and symptomatic HIV. It should be stored at a temperature between 2 to 8 degrees Celsius, as it is sensitive to both heat and light. The vaccine must be discarded 4 hours after reconstitution.

A positive Mantoux or IGRA test indicates only hypersensitivity due to exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It does not affect the level of protection provided by the BCG vaccine. Therefore, these tests are not necessary before administering the vaccine and should not influence the decision to vaccinate.

Note: According to the National Immunization Schedule, the BCG vaccine should be administered at birth, with catch-up vaccination permissible until the age of 1 year. However, the Indian Academy of Paediatrics states that catch-up vaccination is allowed up to 5 years of age.

According to the given data, in country A, the high birth rate has remained unchanged with a decline in the death rate. This will result in an exponential increase in the population. This means country A is in the early expanding stage of the demographic cycle.

In country B, the low birth rate and death rates have remained unchanged. Thus, the population will attain a plateau phase and remain stationary. This means country B is in the low stationary stage of the demographic cycle.

explanationHtml:
In stage 5 of the demographic cycle, the birth rate falls below the death rate.

In this stage, the death rate attains a low stable rate while the birth rate keeps declining. Thus, the curve of the birth rate will cross the curve of the death rate in a graph of the demographic cycle and falls further below.

The demographic gap is negative and the population is declining. So, this stage is known as the declining stage.

The demographic gap refers to the difference between birth rate and death rate which develops when a country undergoes a demographic transition.

In stage 2 of the demographic cycle, the death rate declines but the birth rate remains unchanged. Hence, the demographic gap increases and reaches a maximum by the end of stage 2. In stage 3, both the death rate and birth rate are declining so the demographic gap starts decreasing.

explanationHtml:
The infant mortality rate is not a component of the global hunger index.

The Global Hunger Index (GHI) has three dimensions. These dimensions are measured by indicators.

Dimensions Indicators
Inadequate food supply Proportion of the population undernourished
Child mortality Under 5 mortality rate
Child undernutrition Wasting in children under 5 years
Stunting in children under 5 years

GHI score = (1/3 X standardized PUN) + (1/6 X standardised CWA) + (1/6 X standardised CST) + (1/3 X Standardised CM)

Where,

  • PUN is the proportion of the population that is undernourished
  • CWA is the prevalence of wasting in children under 5 years of age
  • CST is the prevalence of stunting in children under 5 years of age
  • CM is the proportion of children dying under the age of 5 years of age.

The result lies on a scale from 0 to 100, with 0 meaning no hunger and 100 being the worst score. The GHI is given by the International Food Policy Research Institute. In 2021, India's GHI was 27.5. It ranks 101 among 116 countries. In the 2022,India's GHI stands at 29.1, and India ranks 107th out of the 121 countries.

Category

Examples
Water-borne diseases

Caused by ingestion of water contaminated by human or animal faeces, or urine containing pathogenic bacteria or viruses.

explanationHtml:
Microfiltration is a lower-pressure membrane process used for the treatment of water.

Membrane processes are employed in the large scale treatment of water. They are classified as high-pressure processes and lower-pressure processes.

  • High-pressure processes:
    • Reverse osmosis - Rejects monovalent ions and organic molecules of molecular weight > 50 daltons. It is most commonly used for desalination of brackish water and sea water. The membrane pore size is < 0.002 µm.
    • Nanofiltration - Allows monovalent ions such as sodium or potassium to pass but rejects a high proportion of divalent ions like calcium and magnesium and some higher molecular weight organics. The membrane pore size ranges from 0.001 – 0.01 µm.
  • Lower-pressure processes:
    • Ultrafiltration - Rejects organic molecules of molecular weight > 800 daltons. The membrane pore size ranges from 0.002 - 0.03 µm.
    • Microfiltration - Rejects colloidal and suspended material. It does not separate molecules and is usually used before reverse osmosis. The membrane pore size ranges from 0.01 – 12 µm.

In order to estimate the presumptive coliform count, water to be tested is inoculated into tubes containing a suitable liquid medium. These tubes are then incubated and examined after an appropriate period of time. The test is called presumptive because the reaction observed in the tube may occasionally be due to other organisms.

explanationHtml:
Ventilation provided by wind blowing through a space is called perflation.

Ventilation can be broadly classified as natural and mechanical:

Natural ventilation includes:

  • Perflation is the ventilation of a space achieved by allowing wind to blow through it and removing the obstacles for this to happen (e.g., opening windows and doors).
  • Aspiration occurs when there is an obstruction as wind bypasses it and creates a suction action
  • Diffusion is the passage of air through small spaces or openings
  • Cross-ventilation is when air is allowed a natural path through the space by providing openings at appropriate places, opposite each other.

The drawback of natural ventilation is that regulation of air quality is not possible.

Mechanical ventilation includes:

  • Exhaust ventilation utilizes exhaust fans placed high up near the roof on the external walls. A vacuum is created by which fresh air enters the ventilated space.
  • Plenum ventilation uses centrifugal fans to blow fresh air into the room and create a positive pressure, by which vitiated air is pushed out.
  • Balanced ventilation is the combination of both exhaust and plenum methods of ventilation.
  • Air conditioning can be done through mechanical ventilation. It is the simultaneous control of all or at least three factors that influence air quality in a confined room or space. These factors include temperature, humidity, air movement, distribution, dust, bacteria, odours and toxic gases.

correctAnswer: A. Bangalore method is an aerobic process
explanationHtml:
The Bangalore method of composting is an anaerobic process.

Composting is a method of combined disposal of refuse and nightsoil. In this process, organic matter is broken down into compost. It has manure value and few or no disease-causing pathogens.

Bangalore method is an anaerobic method and is also called hot fermentation process. Trenches with a depth of not more than 90cm are used for this. This is done by spreading a layer of refuse (15 cm thick) at the bottom of the trench and nightsoil (5cm thick) is added next. Layers of refuse and nightsoil are added alternatively till the heap rises to 30cm above ground level. The heap is then covered with excavated earth. At the end of 4 – 6 months, decomposition will be completed.

Mechanical composting is an aerobic process. In this method, compost is manufactured on a large scale by processing raw materials and turning out a finished product. The refuse is first cleared of salvageable materials. It is then pulverised to reduce the size of particles to less than 2 inches. The pulverised refuse is then mixed with sewage, sludge or nightsoil in a rotating machine and incubated.

Around 10% to 25% of health care waste is hazardous waste. It may be infectious, toxic, or radioactive in nature. The remaining 75% to 90% is general, non-hazardous waste.

Bio-medical waste means any waste that is generated during:

  • Diagnosis, treatment, or immunization of human beings or animals
  • Research activities pertaining thereto
  • Production or testing of biologicals

Bio-medical waste is handled as per the Bio-medical Waste Management Rules, 2016. However, these rules do not apply to the following:

  • Radioactive wastes
  • Hazardous chemicals
  • Solid wastes
  • Lead-acid batteries
  • Hazardous wastes

  • Hazardous microorganisms

Low-heat system High-heat system

correctAnswer: C. Disaster impact – Response – Rehabilitation – Mitigation
explanationHtml:
The correct order is Disaster impact – Response – Rehabilitation – Mitigation.

Disaster management includes three aspects:

1. Disaster impact and response: It involves immediate management of mass casualties as follows:

  • Search, rescue, and first-aid
  • Field care
  • Triage
  • Tagging
  • Identification of dead

2. Rehabilitation or recovery: It involves the restoration of the pre-disaster conditions by taking steps such as:

  • Water supply
  • Basic sanitation and personal hygiene
  • Food safety
  • Vector control

3. Mitigation: Measures designed either to prevent hazards from causing disaster or to reduce the effects of the disaster. This also includes preparedness for any impending disasters or in disaster-prone areas.

This is used in wars and military settings, where soldiers may need to return to the field of battle soon after treatment. It is also done when there is a scarcity of medical resources after a disaster.

The surge capacity of hospitals is increased to accommodate for the natural disaster, by discharging non-emergent existing patients. This enables hospitals to allow for an acute increase in incoming patients.

correctAnswer: D. A diver who developed decompression sickness
explanationHtml:
Barosinusitis occurs in decompression sickness or Caisson's disease. It is due to the sudden expansion of air in the sinuses.

It can be seen in:

  • Divers who ascend rapidly from deep-sea (high pressure) to the surface of the earth (low pressure)
  • Pilots of unpressurized aircraft or mountaineers who rapidly ascended from the surface of the earth (high-pressure zone) to a high altitude (low-pressure zone)

Under high pressure, gases get compressed, and their solubility increases. When a person is in deep-sea (high-pressure zone) for a long time, an increased amount of nitrogen gets dissolved in his body. When he suddenly comes back to the surface (atmospheric pressure or a low-pressure zone), the solubility of gases decreases and they escape from the dissolved state forming nitrogen bubbles.

These bubbles can cause sudden expansion of air in various parts of the body such as the middle ear (barotitis), sinuses (barosinusitis), beneath teeth (barodontalgia), intestinal loops (abdominal distension), and emphysema.

Nitrogen bubbles can also cause chokes (dyspnoea), bends (joint pain), and prickles (nerve irritation).

The definitive treatment for Caisson's disease is recompression.

explanationHtml:
A study to determine the mean height of children is an example of a descriptive statistical study.

Descriptive statistics are the statistical methods that merely organize, describe or summarize the actual data available. For example, a study determining the mean blood pressure of patients visiting a PHC on a single day.

Analytical statistics are the second major category of epidemiological studies, after descriptive statistics. The objective of an analytical study is to test the hypothesis.

An observational study is an empiric investigation in which the objective is to establish a relationship between cause and effect. It falls under the category of analytical statistics.

It is performed when controlled experimentation cannot be feasibly used to determine a hypothesis. For example, in the case of cigarette smoking causing lung cancer, it would be unethical and not feasible to conduct a controlled experiment. So, an observational study is preferred.

Inferential statistics involve inductive reasoning i.e., generalizing observations to a population after having observed only a sample. An example of such a study would be a study determining the expected success rate of vasectomy

Theoretical statistics is a mathematical approach to describe something, predict events, or analyze the relationship between things. Some of the concepts of theoretical statistics are mean, median, mode, standard deviation and correlation.

An element is a single observation in a study. For example, in a study of blood pressure values, the blood pressure value of one person is an element.

In a statistical study, the population refers to the group about which information is to be gathered. The composition of the population in terms of its age, sex, occupation, cultural characters, etc need to be defined before a study is conducted. The population need not consist of just people but can also be made of measurements. For example, in a study of blood glucose measurements in Indians, the population consists of the blood glucose measurements.

The part/subset of the population, which is being studied is known as a sample. For example, in a questionnaire-based study on cervical cancer in a population, the sample would include females attending the out-patient departments of a hospital. This is a subset of the entire population.

Binomial distribution is widely used in genetic counseling.

Binomial distribution helps determine the probability of occurance of a specific combination of mutually exclusive independent events. In a binomial distribution, there are only two possible events like Yes/No or Male/Female or Alive/Dead. The results of the distribution gives the probabilities of obtaining an exact number of successes in a series of independent trials.

For example, the inheritence of cystic fibrosis follows a binomial distribution. There are:

a. Two possible events - inheriting the disease/ not inheriting it

b. Events are mutually exclusive - one person cannot both have the disease and not have it

c. Independent possibilities - if one child has inherited it, this will not affect if the other child will inherit it.

The physician using this technique can explain to the patients the probabilities of their children suffering from the disease.

explanationHtml:
If the events A and B are mutually exclusive, then the probability of either A or B occuring is given by,

p (A or B) = p (A) + p (B)

This is as per the addition rule of probability.

The probability of both the mutually exclusive events happening at the same time is given by,

p (A and B) = p (A) x p (B)

The probability of any of two mutually non-exclusive events occuring at a point of time is given by,

p (A or B) = p (A) + p (B) - p (A and B)

If p(A) and p(B) are the only two outcomes possible in a given event then,

p (A) + p (B) = 1

For example, probability of patient suffering from lung cancer dying within 5 years and probability of patient suffering from lung cancer surviving these 5 years adds upto 1.

explanationHtml:
The probability that a baby will have a birth weight of < 3kg is 0.70.

In this scenario, the probability of having a baby with BW < 2500 grams, p (A) = 0.50 and that of having a baby with BW between 2500 – 2999 grams, p (B) = 0.20.

Since both events are mutually exclusive, i.e., they cannot happen together, it satisfies the condition for the addition rule of probability.

Thus, the probability of having a baby that weighs less than 3 kilos is,

p (A or B) = p (A) + p (B) = 0.50 + 0.20 = 0.70.

If p(A) and p(B) were non-mutually exclusive events, then the probability would have been calculated by

p(A or B) = p(A) + p(B) - p(A and B).

So, the probability of a person having anemia in the given population (p) = 20/100 = 0.2.

If selecting 3 people from the population randomly, the chance of the first person having anemia is independent of the second or third person also having it and vice versa. This satisfies the condition for the multiplication rule of probability which states that the probability of two or more statistically independent events all occurring together is equal to the product of their individual probabilities.

Thus, here the probability that all the 3 randomly selected people from the population would have anemia = 0.2 x 0.2 x 0.2 = 0.008.

explanationHtml:
The p-value represents the probability of obtaining sample data in the critical region (extreme results) solely by chance when the null hypothesis (H₀) is actually true. In a hypothesis test, the researcher determines a critical region of very unlikely outcomes. If a researcher reports p = 0.03, it means there is only a 3% probability of obtaining that specific sample mean (or one even further into the tails of the distribution) if the null hypothesis is actually true. Since the probability is very low (less than 0.05), the result is considered statistically significant, and the researcher would typically reject the null hypothesis.

Option A: P-value is a probability statement about the sample data, not about the null hypothesis itself. This cannot conclude that there is a 3% probability that H0 is true. Statistical tests provide evidence to support or refute a hypothesis, but they do not provide a direct probability of the hypothesis being true.

Option B: P-value does not measure the probability that the alternative hypothesis (H1) is true. A low p-value suggests the data are inconsistent with H0, which makes H1 more likely, but it does not assign a specific 97% probability to H1.

Option D: A Type II error occurs when a researcher fails to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false. If the researcher rejects the null hypothesis, they are at risk of a Type I error (rejecting a true H0), not a Type II error.

It can more simply be stated as the actual sample size divided by the effective sample size (what you would expect if you were using SRS). For example, let’s say you were using cluster sampling. Among the factors shown in the above statistical group, the odds ratio of early menarche, BRCA mutation, and obesity show positive association and are statistically significant. Hence these 3 factors can be ascertained as risk factors.
High socioeconomic status is not a risk factor. Even though there is a positive association, it is not statistically significant. Any association that has a 95% confidence interval range that includes the value of 1.0 is considered to be non-significant. The value of 1.0 in the range means that the two factors may co-exist together but one is not causing the other to happen.
Odds ratio (OR) is the key parameter in case-control studies to assess the strength of association between the exposure and outcome. The interpretation of the odds ratio can be done as below:
  • OR > 1 indicates a positive association. If both upper and lower limits of the 95% confidence limits are also >1, it suggests that the odds ratio is significant and the factor can be ascertained as a risk factor.
  • OR = 1indicates no association. Irrespective of the odds ratio, if the lower limit of 95% CI is <1 and the upper limit of 95% CI >1, the OR is non-significant and cannot be ascertained either as a protective or a risk factor.
  • OR < 1 indicates a negative association. If both upper and lower limits of the 95% confidence limits are also <1, it suggests that the odds ratio is significant and the factor can be ascertained as a protective factor.

The National Suicide Prevention Strategy (NSPS) aims to reduce suicide mortality by 10% in India by 2030. It is a multisectoral approach that will involve national and international government ministries, families, communities, and educational institutes to help prevent suicide.

India has a high burden of suicide. It is the leading cause of death among individuals between 15-29 years of age.

Epidemiology

  • Young and middle-aged adults between 18-45 years
  • Males more than females
  • Daily wage earners and people who earn <1,00,000 per annum

  • Psychiatric illnesses- Depression, BPD, schizophrenia, and anxiety disorders

  • Major physical illness
  • Job or financial loss
  • Relationship or social loss
  • Domestic violence or abuse
  • Lack of social support
  • The stigma associated with help-seeking behavior of mental disorders
